motion: Can religion and science form a coherent partnership?

referenceDefinitions.label: Appeal to authority
referenceDefinitions.definition: Relying on a person or institution's status as if it settles the argument, especially when the relevant evidence, expertise, or consensus has not been shown.

referenceDefinitions.label: Argument from ignorance
referenceDefinitions.definition: Treating a claim as true because it has not been disproved, or false because it has not been proved, rather than supplying positive evidence.

referenceDefinitions.label: Begging the question
referenceDefinitions.definition: Assuming, directly or indirectly, the very point that needs to be established, so the conclusion is smuggled into the premises.

referenceDefinitions.label: Equivocation
referenceDefinitions.definition: Shifting the meaning of a key word or phrase during the argument, making the reasoning seem stronger than it is.

referenceDefinitions.label: Red herring
referenceDefinitions.definition: Diverting attention from the issue under dispute to a related but less relevant point, leaving the original challenge insufficiently answered.

referenceDefinitions.label: Special pleading
referenceDefinitions.definition: Applying an exception or different standard to one side of the argument without giving a principled reason for the difference.

referenceDefinitions.label: Ambiguity effect
referenceDefinitions.definition: Preferring clearer or more familiar claims over uncertain ones, even when the uncertain option may deserve serious consideration.

referenceDefinitions.label: Authority bias
referenceDefinitions.definition: Giving extra weight to a claim because it comes from a perceived authority, sometimes beyond what the evidence itself supports.

referenceDefinitions.label: Base-rate neglect
referenceDefinitions.definition: Underweighting general background rates or prior probabilities while focusing too heavily on a vivid specific case or local detail.

referenceDefinitions.label: Belief bias
referenceDefinitions.definition: Judging an argument by whether its conclusion feels believable instead of evaluating whether the conclusion follows from the premises.

referenceDefinitions.label: Confirmation bias
referenceDefinitions.definition: Seeking, interpreting, or remembering evidence in ways that favor an existing view while discounting contrary information.

referenceDefinitions.label: Scope neglect
referenceDefinitions.definition: Failing to adjust judgment in proportion to the scale, number, or magnitude of what is being discussed.

referenceDefinitions.label: Subjective validation
referenceDefinitions.definition: Treating a claim as especially accurate or meaningful because it feels personally resonant or confirms one's private experience.

moves.speaker: Jonathan Sacks

sourceSpan.excerpt: Um so it's a privilege. I think where I start and where I've argued in uh in in the great partnership is that Judaism really is a religion that's takes its stand alongside Richard Dawkins. We value the integrity of science. We value an evidence-based approach to natural phenomena. We make a blessing over seeing distinguished scientists. Maimonides says if you want to come to the love and fear of God, study science. Um and I think we also try and do science, I I think care as I mentioned to Richard before, we are One-fifth of a percent of the population of the world. There are only thirteen million Jews in the world. I know we make a lot of noise, but there are actually very few of us. But we have one-twenty percent of the Nobel Prizes in Chemistry, twenty six percent in Physics, twenty seven percent in Medicine and forty one percent in Economics. So we enjoy science and we do it. Um where I think I disagree with Richard is that Richard sees religion and science inevitably in conflict. And I see them as two different sorts of things altogether. Uh science can tell us about the origin of life, religion tells us about the purpose of life. Science explains the world that is, religion summons us to the world that ought to be.

moves.claim: Judaism can stand with science while religion and science answer different kinds of questions.
moves.warrant: Sacks cites an evidence-based approach, a positive religious valuation of scientific study, and distinguishes scientific accounts of origins from religious accounts of purpose and obligation.
moves.inference: Respect for scientific method and a distinct religious role need not place the two practices in inevitable conflict.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly states why scientific integrity and a religious account can coexist.

moves.publicationDescription: Sacks argues that Judaism respects evidence and scientific inquiry while assigning science questions of origins and religion questions of purpose, obligation, and the world humanity ought to build.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Sacks presents an intelligible division of labor through memorable contrasts between origins and purpose, descriptive reality and moral obligation, while grounding compatibility in Jewish esteem for evidence, scientific study, and achievement. Principal limitation: Those examples establish that religious people can value science, but neither Nobel statistics nor appreciative practices independently demonstrate that religion possesses reliable access to purpose, and his portrayal of Dawkins as seeing inevitable conflict compresses the opposing position. Live burden: The partnership still requires a defended account showing why the proposed religious domain is warranted and genuinely coherent with scientific explanation, rather than merely different from it. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins

sourceSpan.excerpt: And I think that what the chief rabbi said about science answering the how questions and religion answering the why questions, that's a very good aspiration. If there was such a thing as a why question, then I guess that would be right. But what I would deny is that why questions are legitimate questions at all. I mean, why questions are fully legitimate when you're talking about human motivation? You ask the question, why did I come to Manchester today? And you'll get an answer, and that's a perfectly sensible question. But if you ask why is there a universe or why are there mountains in the sense of purpose, these are not legitimate questions at all. There's no reason to suppose that why questions have any legitimacy, any right to be asked or answered.

moves.claim: Purpose questions are legitimate for human motivation but are not thereby legitimate questions about the universe.
moves.warrant: Dawkins contrasts an answerable question about why a person traveled with questions that assign purpose to the universe or mountains.
moves.inference: The proposed how-versus-why division does not establish a coherent religious domain unless cosmic why questions are first justified.

burdenContact.rationale: It asks for justification of the religious question-domain rather than assuming it.

responseComponents.rationale: It answers the asserted division between scientific origins and religious purpose by disputing cosmic purpose questions.

moves.publicationDescription: Dawkins distinguishes legitimate questions about human motivation from unsupported questions assigning purpose to mountains or the universe, challenging Sacks to justify religion’s proposed cosmic why-domain.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Dawkins directly identifies the unproved premise beneath Sacks’s proposed partnership, carefully separating answerable questions about a person’s motives from questions that attribute intentional purpose to mountains or the universe. Principal limitation: His examples reveal a missing inferential bridge but do not themselves establish the categorical claim that cosmic why-questions have no legitimacy or even a right to be asked, while the term legitimate remains ambiguous between meaningful, answerable, and evidentially warranted. Live burden: Sacks must justify extending purpose beyond agents, whereas Dawkins must keep his conclusion proportionate to the narrower success of showing that such an extension has not yet been supported. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Jonathan Sacks

sourceSpan.excerpt: But I do none the less value science, because as Richard says, always follow the evidence. And I think there was a lovely story on this just six days ago You know when in 2000 the genome was decoded, it was discovered that only two percent of the genome actually codes for proteins. And as you know, the other ninety eight percent was dismissed as junk junk D_N_A_ Um last week, six days ago, the result of one thousand six hundred experiments by four hundred and fifty scientists in thirty two different institutes institutions discovered that actually that ninety eight percent of people thought was junk isn't junk at all. It's absolutely essential for the maintenance of life. Now for those people who think that ninety eight percent of religion is junk, I hope they might someday rethink that one as well.

moves.claim: Scientific reassessment of so-called junk DNA is offered as an analogy encouraging reassessment of dismissals of religion.
moves.warrant: Sacks says recent research found that genomic material previously dismissed as junk was essential for life, then explicitly transfers that pattern as an analogy to religion.
moves.inference: Past scientific reclassification makes confident wholesale dismissal an attitude worth reconsidering, though the analogy does not itself establish a religious proposition.

burdenContact.rationale: It supports Sacks's request that religion not be dismissed while scientific inquiry is welcomed.

moves.publicationDescription: Sacks compares religion’s dismissal as junk with science’s reassessment of supposedly junk DNA, inviting intellectual humility and reconsideration rather than claiming that genomic research proves religion true.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Sacks uses a concrete and readily understood scientific reclassification to recommend epistemic humility, and he calibrates the comparison as a hope that dismissive critics might reconsider rather than as direct proof of religion. Principal limitation: The shared label junk supplies only a rhetorical resemblance, because discovering biological functions in genomic material offers no relevant evidential bridge to the truth, value, or diversity of religious claims, while ninety-eight percent of religion lacks a defined comparison class. Live burden: To advance the partnership rather than merely discourage contempt, Sacks would need to identify a substantive similarity that makes reassessment transferable and connect it to a specific religious proposition. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Jonathan Sacks

sourceSpan.excerpt: Imagine a visitor, the anthropologist from Mars, who comes along and comes to Manchester and sees the city in the United Blank and sees everyone absolutely at the edge of their seats. As Bill Shankly said, it's much more important than life and death. And wants to know, why are you getting so excited about 22 people chasing this spherical object round a field? In order to explain not the how of football, what are the rules, how do you win, but why people take it so passionately, you've got to step outside of the system. Look at the history of human conflict and the role of games as a substitute conflict. In other words, the meaning of a system lies outside the system, right? Now, if you are a polytheist or you're a Greek philosopher or you're Richard Dawkins, you don't believe there is anything outside the system. There is nothing outside the universe, so there is no why. Whereas we believe that there is a God who transcends the universe, therefore there is a why. Ultimately, is the universe meaningful or meaningless? This is probably going to divide Richard and myself.

moves.claim: Meaning for a system can lie outside that system, so belief in a transcendent God permits a cosmic why.
moves.warrant: The football example distinguishes rules internal to a game from the wider human history that explains why people care; Sacks then maps that distinction onto the universe and transcendence.
moves.inference: If God transcends the universe, the universe can have meaning not captured by its internal physical description.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies the proposed bridge from transcendence to cosmic purpose.

responseComponents.rationale: It challenges the restriction of purpose to human motivation by proposing an external source of systemic meaning.

moves.publicationDescription: Using football’s significance beyond its internal rules, Sacks argues that systems may receive meaning from a wider context and that a transcendent God could therefore ground cosmic purpose.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Sacks answers Dawkins’s restriction of purpose to human motivation with a lucid football example showing that internal rules can leave a practice’s significance unexplained, thereby supplying an intelligible model of externally grounded meaning. Principal limitation: Football sits within a known social world, whereas the universe’s exterior and transcendent source are precisely disputed, so the analogy illustrates a conditional possibility without independently establishing its antecedent and shifts meaning from human significance toward cosmic purpose. Live burden: Sacks must warrant both an outside to the universe and the inference from that transcendence to purpose, while distinguishing cosmic meaning from the significance humans confer upon practices. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins

sourceSpan.excerpt: The parable of football, of course, works for human affairs, but it is human affairs. That's what I meant when I said that meaning in the sense of purpose works for human affairs. But as you've said, Chief Rabbi, the whole question is, does it work? for non-human affairs? Does it work for the universe? Actually, I mean, it sort of works for animals and plants because the Darwinian rationale gives a kind of meaning to purpose, the purpose of a bird's wing. It flies, and that keeps the bird alive, which passes the bird's genes on. So that's another kind of metaphorical usage of the word purpose. But ultimate purpose, it's no good just giving us parables about football. You have to actually give a reason to suppose that there is some kind of purpose in the physical universe. And I've never seen any such reason. So I think the onus is on you to provide a reason why we should think that.

moves.claim: The football analogy works for human affairs but gives no reason to infer ultimate purpose in the physical universe.
moves.warrant: Dawkins distinguishes human motivation and evolved functional purpose from ultimate purpose and explicitly requests evidence for the latter.
moves.inference: An analogy grounded in human practices cannot carry the evidential burden of establishing cosmic purpose.

burdenContact.rationale: It distinguishes accepted uses of purpose language from the disputed cosmic use.

responseComponents.rationale: It denies that the football comparison supplies a reason for purpose in the universe.

moves.publicationDescription: Dawkins grants purpose in human motivation and evolved biological function but argues that neither football nor bird wings supplies evidence for ultimate purpose in the physical universe.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Dawkins precisely distinguishes three uses of purpose—human motivation, biological function, and ultimate cosmic intention—and explains why the football and bird-wing cases do not entail the disputed third category. Principal limitation: The reply is principally diagnostic rather than a comprehensive naturalistic explanation, and its claim that he has never encountered a reason adds personal testimony without strengthening the rigorous burden analysis, although no contrary worldview burden belongs to him here. Live burden: Sacks must provide independent support for cosmic purpose instead of another human analogy, while Dawkins’s narrower task is to preserve the distinction and assess any offered bridge fairly. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Jonathan Sacks

sourceSpan.excerpt: The reason why we should think it is when you step back and say, now, why does the universe exist? Now, that's not a scientific question. I agree with you. It's absolutely not. But why would an infinite creator who, by definition, lacks nothing create a universe? And the short answer that Judaism gives, the Abrahamic monotheisms give, is that God created the universe out of love. Love seeks to create otherness. And therefore, the simplest answer I would give is that God created the universe in love and forgiveness, asking us to love and forgive others.

moves.claim: Judaism answers the non-scientific question of creation's purpose by saying an infinite creator created out of love and calls humans to love and forgiveness.
moves.warrant: Sacks reasons that an infinite creator lacks nothing, identifies love as seeking otherness, and presents creation and moral summons as connected.
moves.inference: Within the stated theistic frame, love supplies the proposed purpose for creation.

burdenContact.rationale: It articulates the positive purpose account while acknowledging that it is not a scientific answer.

responseComponents.rationale: It supplies the reason Sacks says Judaism gives for cosmic purpose.

moves.publicationDescription: Sacks offers Judaism’s explicitly non-scientific explanation that an infinite creator, lacking nothing, created out of love, with creation’s purpose expressed through human love and forgiveness.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Sacks responds with a theological account rather than evasion, labels it non-scientific, and constructs an intelligible sequence from an infinite creator’s lack of need through love’s pursuit of otherness to obligations of love and forgiveness. Principal limitation: The account assumes the creator whose existence is contested, supplies no warrant for the assertion that love seeks otherness, and compresses the transition from a motive for creation to the prescribed human moral response. Live burden: Sacks must provide reason to accept the creator premise and explain why love is the uniquely fitting purpose, rather than reporting what Abrahamic traditions answer once that framework is granted. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins

sourceSpan.excerpt: Well, yes, because when you say, why would God do it? I mean, that, of course, presupposes God's there in the first place. And that's the whole issue. So it's not good enough to say, why would God do it and do it out of love? I mean, if you want to do that, then I would start to get a bit curious about why he waited 14 billion years before humans came on the scene.

moves.claim: Explaining why God created out of love presupposes the disputed existence of God.
moves.warrant: Dawkins points out that the form of Sacks's question begins with God already in place and adds the long delay before humans as a reason for further curiosity.
moves.inference: The offered purpose account cannot independently warrant the creator on which it depends.

burdenContact.rationale: It asks whether the specifically religious premise is independently supported.

responseComponents.rationale: It argues that the creator invoked by the warrant is assumed rather than established.

moves.publicationDescription: Dawkins argues that asking why God created from love already assumes God exists, so the proposed motive cannot independently establish the creator or cosmic purpose it presupposes.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Dawkins isolates the exact logical dependency in Sacks’s answer, distinguishing an explanation of why an assumed creator acted from independent support for whether that creator exists, and he does so using the opponent’s own formulation. Principal limitation: The fourteen-billion-year timing aside expresses understandable curiosity but remains suggestive because its evidential significance is not developed, adding little to the exceptionally focused presupposition objection and risking distraction from the decisive point. Live burden: Sacks must establish the creator premise without relying on a question that already embeds it, while Dawkins need not furnish a complete naturalistic cosmology to expose that circular explanatory structure. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Jonathan Sacks

sourceSpan.excerpt: The National Maritime Institute in America in September 2010 published, and you can still find it on the web, a computer simulation of the Red Sea, a particular point in the bitter lakes in the Nile Delta, at which a 63-mile-an-hour east wind would part the waters.

moves.claim: A cited computer simulation supplies a natural mechanism by which the Red Sea's waters could part.
moves.warrant: Sacks identifies a simulation locating the event near the Bitter Lakes in the Nile Delta and specifying a 63-mile-an-hour east wind as sufficient to part the waters.
moves.inference: The Red Sea example can be described using a concrete scientific mechanism rather than only a mechanism-free supernatural account.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers a worked example in which a scriptural event is paired with a proposed natural mechanism.

responseComponents.rationale: It answers the Red Sea test case with a specific proposed scientific mechanism.

moves.publicationDescription: Sacks cites a computer simulation in which a sixty-three-mile-per-hour east wind at the Bitter Lakes parts water, offering a natural mechanism compatible with the Red Sea narrative.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Sacks answers the Red Sea test case with concrete conditions—a Bitter Lakes location, east wind, specified speed, and computer simulation—showing how a scriptural event could be physically compatible with a natural mechanism. Principal limitation: A model of physical possibility neither confirms that the narrated event historically occurred nor explains why this narrative should be classified literally, and the damaged institutional attribution plus unexamined study limits verification despite the proposal’s specificity. Live burden: Sacks must separate compatibility from historical evidence and supply the general interpretive rule Dawkins requested, rather than allowing a possible mechanism to carry both classification and occurrence. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins

sourceSpan.excerpt: No, I mean, I would say I have a bigger worry with literalism. And that is a big problem. We don't have it so much in this country. But in America, it's a very serious problem. And so serious theologians like the Chief Rabbi who don't take it literally are, as it were, less of a problem. But as a matter of fact, I have been quite surprised at, I mean, people have always been tackling me for saying, why do you go for the easy target? Why do you go for the low-hanging fruit, the creationist idiots? So you ought to be tackling serious theologians. Well, I've been talking to some serious theologians, and I'm quite surprised how close to literalists some of them are. I mean, some of them, I've met bishops who actually believe Jesus turned water into wine and that kind of thing. So I'm not sure there's that much difference between the low-hanging fruit. And I mean, what about the burning bush and parting of the Red Sea and things? Is that symbolic, or is that literal?

moves.claim: Literalism is the larger concern, but some serious theologians remain close to literalism, as concrete miracle claims illustrate.
moves.warrant: Dawkins contrasts symbolic interpreters with creationists, reports encountering bishops who affirm miracles, and asks whether the burning bush and Red Sea are symbolic or literal.
moves.inference: A nonliteral religious approach still needs a consistent account of how its literal claims are selected.

burdenContact.rationale: It requests a rule separating literal from symbolic religious claims.

moves.publicationDescription: Dawkins distinguishes Sacks from creationist literalists, but tests the distinction by asking whether miracle narratives such as the burning bush and Red Sea are symbolic or literal.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Dawkins turns a general concern about literalism into concrete interpretive test cases, asking how burning-bush and Red-Sea narratives are classified and thereby exposing the need for a consistently defensible selection method. Principal limitation: His supporting generalization rests on undefined categories and anecdotal encounters with bishops, while the disparaging comparison to creationist “idiots” weakens charitable differentiation among theologians without demonstrating actual inconsistency. Live burden: Sacks still must explain which principle separates literal from symbolic claims, whereas Dawkins has not established that sophisticated nonliteral interpretation lacks such a principle or that his examples represent serious theology broadly. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Jonathan Sacks

sourceSpan.excerpt: Well, Adam and Eve is clearly a parable because there was no first human.

moves.claim: Adam and Eve should be read as a parable rather than as the first biological humans.
moves.warrant: Sacks says there was no first human.
moves.inference: The absence of a discrete first human supplies a reason not to treat Adam and Eve as a literal account of the first biological pair.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies a source-backed reason for treating this particular narrative nonliterally.

moves.publicationDescription: Sacks classifies Adam and Eve as a parable because evolutionary continuity supplies no discrete first biological human, making a literal first-pair reading scientifically untenable.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Sacks answers the requested test case directly and connects his parable classification to a scientifically pertinent premise, because gradual human evolution provides no discrete first biological individual corresponding to a literal original pair. Principal limitation: The compressed assertion leaves the evolutionary premise unexplained and does not yet demonstrate that the same interpretive method governs other narratives rather than only resolving this especially straightforward incompatibility. Live burden: He must supply a general, consistently applicable classification rule and show how it handles harder cases, while Dawkins would need to contest either the no-first-human premise or its relevance to literal interpretation. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins

sourceSpan.excerpt: Adam and Eve is symbolic, but the parting of the Red Sea. I mean, how do you decide which bits are symbolic?

moves.claim: Calling Adam and Eve symbolic while treating the Red Sea as literal requires a rule for deciding between the classifications.
moves.warrant: Dawkins states the two contrasting classifications and immediately asks how the symbolic portions are selected.
moves.inference: The contrasting classifications need an explicit and consistently applicable interpretive criterion.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly asks for the criterion that separates symbolic from literal narratives.

responseComponents.rationale: It contrasts the treatment of the Red Sea example with the separately stated Adam-and-Eve classification and asks for the governing rule.

moves.publicationDescription: Dawkins contrasts symbolic Adam and Eve with a literal Red Sea and asks Sacks for the general rule that warrants these differing classifications.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Dawkins precisely juxtaposes Sacks’s adjacent classifications of Adam and Eve and the Red Sea, then asks for the missing criterion instead of prematurely declaring the two interpretations inconsistent. Principal limitation: The conversationally compressed contrast identifies a methodological gap but supplies no independent argument that the classifications cannot be reconciled once an explicit scientific or interpretive rule is stated. Live burden: Sacks must articulate a stable principle that explains the divergent treatments and can govern comparable cases, while Dawkins retains responsibility for testing that principle rather than treating the request itself as a refutation. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Jonathan Sacks

sourceSpan.excerpt: Very simple. The rabbis in the 10th century laid down the following principle. If a biblical narrative is incompatible with established scientific fact, it is not to be read literally. And that was eight centuries before the word scientist was coined. So they weren't just doing it to please Richard Dawkins. They were doing it for their own intellectual integrity.

moves.claim: A biblical narrative incompatible with established scientific fact should not be read literally.
moves.warrant: Sacks attributes this principle to tenth-century rabbis and notes that it predates the modern term scientist.
moves.inference: The literal-symbolic distinction can be governed by an established interpretive rule responsive to scientific knowledge.

burdenContact.rationale: It states the method used to reconcile interpretation with established science.

responseComponents.rationale: It directly supplies the requested classification rule.

moves.publicationDescription: Sacks answers that any biblical narrative incompatible with established scientific fact should be read nonliterally, presenting this as a longstanding rabbinic principle of intellectual integrity.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Sacks supplies exactly the requested criterion in a clear conditional form, linking established scientific incompatibility to nonliteral interpretation and explaining why Adam and Eve receive a different treatment from scientifically possible narratives. Principal limitation: His tenth-century attribution is unsupported within the exchange, and the rule leaves unresolved how to classify stories that are scientifically compatible yet historically unverified, metaphorical, or otherwise interpretively contested. Live burden: Sacks must defend the historical provenance, specify what qualifies as established fact and genuine incompatibility, and explain decisions outside that boundary, while Dawkins must test rather than ignore the offered rule. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Jonathan Sacks

sourceSpan.excerpt: I believe it literally happened. And I believe that whole narrative was critically misunderstood. with disastrous consequences. But here I'm going to make a very strong statement. We know the Bible regards the worst sin of all, and it runs through all the prophetic books as child sacrifice. Furthermore, we know child sacrifice actually happened on a massive scale. All the archaeological digs at Carthage, as well as the Mayans and Aztecs, with all the ancient societies, performed child sacrifice. And we know well into Roman law there was a principle of patria potestas, which says a child is the property of its parents, and therefore a parent can dispose of a child as he wishes. And God is saying to Abraham, this child for whom you've waited. You remember all those years they were waiting for a child, just one child. This child for whom you're waiting, I want you to give him back to me. The second Abraham disowns Isaac, God says right now, have him back. But know that you are his guardian, not his owner. Every child belongs to me. In other words, a parent may not sacrifice a child. The Bible is an extended polemic against child sacrifice.

moves.claim: The Abraham and Isaac narrative is a polemic against child sacrifice rather than an endorsement of it.
moves.warrant: Sacks points to biblical condemnation of child sacrifice, its prevalence in ancient societies, and legal treatment of children as parental property.
moves.inference: The story's historical setting supports reading it as a rejection of parental ownership and sacrifice.

burdenContact.rationale: It applies Sacks's interpretive approach to a morally difficult narrative.

moves.publicationDescription: Sacks reads Abraham and Isaac as an anti-sacrifice polemic, using ancient sacrificial practices and parental ownership norms to infer that parents are guardians, not owners.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Sacks offers a substantive historical-moral interpretation, connecting ancient child sacrifice and parental property norms to the narrative’s reversal and its vivid guardian-not-owner conclusion. Principal limitation: His archaeological, legal, and biblical generalizations are compressed and undocumented here, while the confident claim that this is the story’s controlling meaning does not sufficiently examine rival readings or justify the ordeal itself. Live burden: He must substantiate the historical setting and show why the terrifying command is a proportionate vehicle for repudiating sacrifice, whereas Dawkins must engage the anti-sacrifice context rather than merely restating revulsion. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins

sourceSpan.excerpt: Why, why, why? If God wanted to tell Abraham and tell the Jews not to sacrifice children, why didn't he just tell them? I mean, why put Abraham and Isaac through that horrific ordeal in order to make a symbolic gesture?

moves.claim: If the intended lesson was not to sacrifice children, God could have stated it directly rather than subjecting Abraham and Isaac to a horrific ordeal.
moves.warrant: Dawkins contrasts direct instruction with the elaborate test and questions why the ordeal was needed to make the symbolic point.
moves.inference: The proposed moral interpretation does not by itself justify the narrative means used to convey it.

burdenContact.rationale: It tests whether the proposed moral reading makes coherent sense of the story's form.

responseComponents.rationale: It grants the stated lesson for purposes of objection but challenges the means by which the story conveys it.

moves.publicationDescription: Dawkins grants Sacks’s proposed anti-sacrifice lesson for argument’s sake but asks why direct prohibition could not replace the horrific ordeal imposed on Abraham and Isaac.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Dawkins conditionally accepts Sacks’s intended anti-sacrifice lesson and isolates the decisive unresolved issue by contrasting straightforward divine instruction with the terrifying ordeal imposed on Abraham and Isaac. Principal limitation: The objection establishes a plausible less harmful alternative but does not yet engage historical reasons why a dramatic reversal might communicate more effectively than a bare prohibition within a sacrifice-normalizing culture. Live burden: Sacks must justify the narrative mechanism’s necessity or proportionality, while Dawkins must answer any culturally grounded account of why direct instruction would have lacked comparable force without conceding that effectiveness settles morality. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Jonathan Sacks

sourceSpan.excerpt: I'll tell you why. Because every self-respecting God in those days, Ra, Kamosh, Baal, and all the rest of them said sacrifice your child. So if God said to Abraham, Abraham, don't sacrifice your child, Abraham might have found that pretty hard to take. But taking him all the way up there and then slamming on the brakes left an impression on Jews, not just on Abraham, to this day that we have become a child-focused religion.

moves.claim: The dramatic command and reversal made the prohibition memorable in a culture where gods were expected to demand child sacrifice.
moves.warrant: Sacks says other deities demanded child sacrifice, so a bare contrary instruction could have been difficult for Abraham to accept; taking the action to the brink and stopping it left a lasting impression.
moves.inference: The ordeal's form is explained as a culturally situated way to reverse an entrenched norm.

burdenContact.rationale: It connects the narrative form to the historical function claimed for the story.

responseComponents.rationale: It explains why Sacks thinks direct instruction would have been less effective in that setting.

moves.publicationDescription: Sacks argues that a dramatic command followed by last-moment reversal could overturn entrenched sacrificial expectations more memorably than a bare prohibition and shape a child-focused tradition.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Sacks directly answers why a bare prohibition might fail, proposing that an expected sacrificial command followed by abrupt reversal would memorably overturn an entrenched cultural norm and explain the story’s enduring pedagogical force. Principal limitation: The mechanism remains conjectural because he does not substantiate Abraham’s likely psychology, the universality of surrounding divine demands, or the claimed causal path from narrative drama to a child-focused religious tradition. Live burden: He must show that this effectiveness account is historically grounded and morally proportionate, while Dawkins must distinguish communicative memorability from justification without overlooking the contextual explanation. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins

sourceSpan.excerpt: I'm delighted to hear that. But the original story seems to me to be the most appalling child abuse, child abuse.

moves.claim: Even if the later religious tradition is child-focused, the original story presents appalling child abuse.
moves.warrant: Dawkins expressly welcomes the claimed child-focused outcome but separates that outcome from his judgment about what Isaac undergoes in the narrative.
moves.inference: A beneficial later interpretation does not remove the moral objection to the depicted ordeal itself.

burdenContact.rationale: It maintains a moral-coherence objection after acknowledging Sacks's claimed outcome.

responseComponents.rationale: It denies that the story's claimed effectiveness resolves the moral objection to the ordeal.

moves.publicationDescription: Dawkins welcomes the claimed child-focused legacy but maintains that the original narrative still depicts appalling child abuse, separating beneficial reception from the ordeal’s morality.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Dawkins explicitly welcomes Sacks’s claimed child-focused legacy before sharply separating that beneficial later outcome from the moral character of Isaac’s ordeal within the original narrative. Principal limitation: Calling the episode the “most appalling child abuse” communicates the judgment forcefully but offers little analysis of Isaac’s experience, no defended comparative standard, and no direct answer to Sacks’s culturally situated effectiveness mechanism. Live burden: Dawkins must explain why pedagogical success cannot proportionately justify the depicted terror, while Sacks must show more than lasting influence if he wants the reversal to resolve the moral objection. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Jonathan Sacks

sourceSpan.excerpt: I agree with you, Richard. And you are reading it. Forgive me for saying this, the Christian way.

moves.claim: Sacks agrees that the story is abusive under the reading Dawkins applies but attributes that result to a different interpretive tradition.
moves.warrant: He explicitly says he agrees and then says Dawkins is reading it 'the Christian way.'
moves.inference: The remaining dispute is framed as one about interpretation rather than whether child abuse would be appalling.

burdenContact.rationale: It clarifies that Sacks locates the disagreement in the governing interpretation.

responseComponents.rationale: It concedes the abuse description under Dawkins's reading while disputing that reading.

moves.publicationDescription: Sacks accepts that Dawkins's reading depicts abuse, but relocates their disagreement to interpretation by characterizing that reading as specifically Christian.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Sacks directly concedes the moral force of Dawkins's child-abuse judgment under the interpretation being applied, thereby identifying interpretation, rather than indifference to Isaac's ordeal, as their remaining disagreement. Principal limitation: Merely calling that interpretation Christian neither explains the relevant doctrinal difference nor demonstrates how Sacks's alternative reading removes the frightening treatment that Dawkins isolated. Live burden: He still needs to articulate a principled interpretive account that preserves his anti-sacrifice lesson while answering why the narrated ordeal remains morally coherent, and he offers no source-based support for assigning the rival reading to Christianity generally. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Jonathan Sacks

sourceSpan.excerpt: Secondly, though, I quoted in the book the evidence here, because Robert Putnam, the professor of sociology at Harvard, did all the research on this. And he came up with this extraordinary finding, as you know, that in America, it may not be true in Britain, although he tells me it is in Britain, that religious people are more likely to give to charity, more likely to do voluntary work, more likely to help a neighbor with housework, more likely to help somebody with a job, more likely to get involved in civic and voluntary associations, and so on. And his finding was that religion is the predictor of all these things, of altruism, more than any other factor, age, income, educational level, or ethnicity. But he said, and I think very wisely, that in his view, this has got nothing to do with religious beliefs and everything to do with the power of religion to create communities.

moves.claim: Research is presented as showing that religious participation predicts several forms of altruistic and civic conduct, with community rather than belief as the mechanism.
moves.warrant: Sacks attributes the findings to Robert Putnam, lists charitable, voluntary, neighborly, employment, and civic activities, and says the reported relationship exceeds several demographic factors.
moves.inference: Religion's community-forming capacity can have socially relevant effects even if the causal mechanism is not doctrinal belief.

burdenContact.rationale: It connects religion to civic outcomes through community formation.

moves.publicationDescription: Sacks cites Robert Putnam's research linking religious participation with charitable, voluntary, neighborly, and civic activity, while attributing the association to community formation rather than belief.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Sacks supplies a named researcher, multiple concrete measures of altruistic and civic conduct, relevant demographic comparisons, and a carefully bounded mechanism that locates the apparent benefit in community formation rather than religious doctrine. Principal limitation: The excerpt provides no study design, effect sizes, controls, or rival-cause analysis, while the word predictor leaves association and causation insufficiently distinguished and the suggested British generalization remains qualified. Live burden: This evidence supports religion's socially consequential community role, but Sacks still must show whether the association is robust across settings and whether religious institutions produce something distinctive that comparably organized secular communities cannot reproduce. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins

sourceSpan.excerpt: what the chief rabbis just said, that it's not religion per se, but it's a sense of community. Before accepting the findings, I think I would want to look a little bit in more detail at what's going on there. The giving to charity, if the charity includes tithing in the broad sense, I mean, giving to a church, then.

moves.claim: The community finding warrants closer inspection, including whether measured charity includes giving to a church.
moves.warrant: Dawkins accepts the distinction between religion itself and community, then identifies tithing or church giving as a possible measurement issue.
moves.inference: The empirical comparison should not be accepted without checking what is counted as charitable giving.

burdenContact.rationale: It tests whether the evidence specifically supports the claimed community benefit.

responseComponents.rationale: It questions the operational definition of one reported altruism measure.

moves.publicationDescription: Dawkins provisionally accepts the community mechanism but asks whether charitable giving includes church contributions, arguing that the reported religious advantage requires closer measurement scrutiny.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Dawkins grants Sacks's distinction between religion and community, then identifies a precise measurement question—whether tithing or church contributions count as charity—that could materially affect interpretation of the reported religious advantage. Principal limitation: He does not establish that such giving was actually included, quantify its possible influence, or complete the conditional sentence by specifying exactly how the comparison would be distorted. Live burden: As a diagnostic critic, he need only justify closer inspection rather than prove an opposing social theory, but the concern remains provisional until the measure's definition and outcome sensitivity are examined. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Jonathan Sacks

sourceSpan.excerpt: No, no. Whether religious or secular causes, absolutely exclusive.

moves.claim: Sacks says the reported charity finding covers both religious and secular causes.
moves.warrant: He answers Dawkins's measurement question with the narrow clarification, 'Whether religious or secular causes,' followed by an affirmation.
moves.inference: As Sacks describes it, the reported association is not limited to only religious causes or only secular causes; the reply does not establish whether church giving is included or excluded.

burdenContact.rationale: It clarifies the stated breadth of causes covered by the charity finding without overstating what the reply establishes.

responseComponents.rationale: It supplies a limited clarification about the causes covered while leaving the church-giving inclusion question unresolved.

moves.publicationDescription: Sacks answers that the charity evidence covers both religious and secular causes, offering breadth of coverage without resolving whether church giving itself was included.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Sacks gives a direct, intelligible clarification that the reported charitable activity covers religious as well as secular causes, so the measure is not described as confined to one category of beneficiary. Principal limitation: That breadth does not answer Dawkins's narrower question about whether church giving was included, how categories were defined, or whether such contributions materially drove the association, and no study documentation accompanies the assertion. Live burden: Sacks must show whether church giving was included and how its inclusion affected the reported association, questions that the breadth clarification leaves unresolved. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins

sourceSpan.excerpt: I want to pursue the very interesting point you were making, that it's the sense of community rather than, and that, I think, is an arguably good point. I certainly don't think we get our morals from religion. I certainly hope we don't. I mean, I hope we don't get them from scripture. I certainly hope that. And I also hope we don't get them from a kind of feeling of sucking up to God. And I'm sure you would agree about that. So do we get it from a sense of community? That's an interesting point.

moves.claim: The community rather than belief explanation is an arguable and interesting account of the social effect.
moves.warrant: Dawkins explicitly returns to and provisionally accepts the community point, while separating it from claims that morality comes from religion or scripture.
moves.inference: A social benefit can be acknowledged without treating religious doctrine as its necessary source.

burdenContact.rationale: It accepts community as a candidate mechanism while denying that religion is therefore the source of morality.

responseComponents.rationale: It accepts the community mechanism as arguable but resists a doctrinal conclusion.

moves.publicationDescription: Dawkins grants that community may plausibly explain the reported social effect while separating that concession from any claim that religion or scripture supplies morality.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Dawkins explicitly returns to Sacks's strongest empirical mechanism, calls it arguable and interesting, and cleanly distinguishes a community-produced social effect from the stronger conclusion that religious doctrine or scripture is morality's necessary source. Principal limitation: His provisional acceptance relies on Sacks's reported account without comparing religious and nonreligious communities, while the repeated remarks about unwanted moral sources broaden beyond the immediate empirical question without additional support. Live burden: To advance the secular alternative further, he must show that community alone explains the association and that comparable institutions can preserve the relevant benefits without the religious setting. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Jonathan Sacks

sourceSpan.excerpt: You're looking forward to a post-religious age, but then scientists in the 18th century were looking forward to it. Why didn't it appear?

moves.claim: Earlier expectations of a post-religious age were not fulfilled, so the expectation of religion's disappearance calls for explanation.
moves.warrant: Sacks notes that eighteenth-century scientists also anticipated such an age and asks why it did not arrive.
moves.inference: The persistence of religion is evidence against treating a post-religious future as straightforward or imminent.

burdenContact.rationale: It raises religion's historical persistence as relevant to claims of replacement.

responseComponents.rationale: It questions the expectation that a post-religious setting will materialize.

moves.publicationDescription: Sacks challenges Dawkins's expected post-religious future by noting that eighteenth-century scientists anticipated the same outcome and asking why religion nevertheless persisted.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Sacks targets the temporal assumption inside Dawkins's proposal, using the failure of earlier post-religious expectations to demand an explanation rather than simply asserting that eventual secularization is impossible. Principal limitation: The historical claim names no scientists, dates, regions, measures, or threshold for a post-religious age, and continued persistence cannot by itself establish that religion will not decline later. Live burden: He still must explain what sustained religion, show why those conditions undermine Dawkins's forecast, and connect persistence to religion's distinctive community value rather than merely to its historical durability. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins

sourceSpan.excerpt: I think it's an interesting point, and I think it's arguable that in the post-religious age, which I look forward to, we're going to need to put in place some sort of substitute for the sense of community, which religions over centuries of history have put in place.

moves.claim: A post-religious society may need to create a substitute for the sense of community religions have historically supplied.
moves.warrant: Dawkins treats the community benefit as arguable and anticipates preserving that function through another institution in a post-religious age.
moves.inference: The acknowledged community function does not establish that religion itself is irreplaceable.

burdenContact.rationale: It proposes functional replacement rather than denying the historical community role.

moves.publicationDescription: Dawkins proposes that a post-religious society create a substitute for the community religions historically provided, treating the social function as valuable but potentially replaceable.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Dawkins converts his concession about religion's centuries-long community role into a coherent functional distinction: if community produces the benefit, another institution could in principle preserve that benefit without requiring religious belief. Principal limitation: He names no candidate institution, comparative precedent, transition mechanism, or evidence that a secular substitute could match religious communities at scale, while post-religious age remains an undefined expectation. Live burden: The proposal must become more than conceptual possibility by specifying how replacement communities would form, endure, motivate participation, and reproduce the relevant altruistic and civic outcomes across populations. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins

sourceSpan.excerpt: Well, I think the broad sweep of history is in the right direction. It's a sawtooth sort of zigzagging up on the way. We have our temporary reverses, but we're generally heading in the right direction, as polls suggest.

moves.claim: Despite temporary reverses, the broad historical trend is moving in the anticipated direction.
moves.warrant: Dawkins characterizes the trend as a sawtooth progression and appeals to polls as support.
moves.inference: Past failure to reach a post-religious age does not defeat the longer-term secular forecast.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends the plausibility of a future secular alternative despite historical delay.

responseComponents.rationale: It argues that persistence to date is compatible with a longer-term secular trend.

moves.publicationDescription: Dawkins answers religion's persistence by describing secularization as a long-term sawtooth trend, with temporary reversals compatible with the broad direction allegedly indicated by polls.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Dawkins offers a coherent trend-based answer to Sacks's persistence challenge, explaining that temporary reversals can coexist with a longer secular trajectory instead of treating historical change as smooth or immediate. Principal limitation: His appeal to polls supplies no geography, period, measure, results, or definition of secularization, and the sawtooth model can absorb contrary observations too easily unless its direction and reversal conditions are independently specified. Live burden: He must document the claimed broad trend, explain the historical delay Sacks identified, and show that declining religiosity would enable effective replacement of religion's acknowledged community functions. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Jonathan Sacks

sourceSpan.excerpt: I think we agree on the integrity of science, on the power that it has given us, and the immense dignity that it represents. Richard accepts that as a fact. I accept that as what the Bible means when it says God made us in his image. But nonetheless, we both cherish science as one of the great human achievements.

moves.claim: Both speakers cherish the integrity, power, dignity, and achievement of science, though Sacks also gives that dignity a biblical interpretation.
moves.warrant: Sacks states their agreement about science, notes Dawkins accepts it as fact, and connects his own acceptance to humanity being made in God's image.
moves.inference: Religious interpretation can be layered onto a shared valuation of science without denying that valuation.

burdenContact.rationale: It identifies the shared foundation on which Sacks's partnership claim rests.

moves.publicationDescription: Sacks says both speakers cherish science’s integrity, power, dignity, and achievements, while his biblical image-of-God reading adds a religious interpretation to their shared esteem.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Sacks identifies common ground in both speakers’ respect for science, distinguishes Dawkins’s factual acceptance from his biblical interpretation, and supports compatibility without attributing religious agreement to Dawkins. Principal limitation: Their shared esteem establishes neither the truth nor the warrant of the image-of-God interpretation, while the move shifts from science’s dignity to a theological explanation whose evidential basis remains asserted. Live burden: To advance the partnership beyond appreciation, Sacks must show why the religious layer supplies justified explanation instead of an interpretation superimposed upon scientific achievement, especially given the dispute over supernatural warrant. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins

sourceSpan.excerpt: We're both very nice people. And we share with many other people a sense of goodwill towards humanity and, indeed, towards sentient beings generally. We would agree about a very large number of moral questions if actually faced with them, if there's a particular dilemma. I don't think we would ever agree about the legitimacy, the role of supernatural explanations for anything. And as a scientist, I'm interested in that. And I think that we are poles apart on that.

moves.claim: The speakers share goodwill and likely answers to many moral dilemmas while remaining divided over supernatural explanations.
moves.warrant: Dawkins identifies goodwill toward humanity and sentient beings, predicts agreement on concrete moral questions, and separately marks supernatural explanation as the enduring disagreement.
moves.inference: Moral common ground is possible without agreement on religious explanatory claims.

burdenContact.rationale: It separates moral agreement from endorsement of supernatural explanation.

moves.publicationDescription: Dawkins says shared goodwill and likely moral agreement can coexist with a decisive divide over whether supernatural explanations have any legitimate role.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Dawkins answers the request for common ground, separating agreement on moral dilemmas from disagreement about supernatural explanation, while crediting Sacks with goodwill toward humanity and sentient beings. Principal limitation: The claimed moral agreement remains hypothetical because no dilemma is tested, and his statement that supernatural explanations lack a role for anything makes the boundary broader than this exchange independently demonstrates. Live burden: Dawkins must defend that explanatory exclusion rather than merely state it, while preserving the distinction that moral cooperation neither requires nor establishes shared religious premises. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].

moves.speaker: Jonathan Sacks

sourceSpan.excerpt: And it is my belief that we will always need a sense of that which is beyond us in order, A, to never lose sight of human dignity. The thing that really scares me is the kind of scientist like BF Skinner, the behavioral psychologist who wrote this book called Beyond Freedom and Dignity. I think freedom and dignity and hope are the three things for which it's very hard to find scientific evidence.

moves.claim: Science should be cherished, but a sense of transcendence is still needed to preserve human dignity, freedom, and hope.
moves.warrant: Sacks cites concern about a scientific outlook exemplified by a work titled Beyond Freedom and Dignity and notes the difficulty of finding scientific evidence for freedom, dignity, and hope.
moves.inference: Scientific achievement and a transcendent moral frame are presented as complementary rather than exhaustive alternatives.

burdenContact.rationale: It links transcendence to values Sacks says scientific evidence alone does not establish.

responseComponents.rationale: It agrees on practical and scientific common ground while stating why Sacks retains a transcendent framework.

moves.publicationDescription: Sacks argues that science deserves admiration, yet transcendence remains necessary to protect human dignity, freedom, and hope because those values resist straightforward scientific evidence.
moves.publicationCritique: Strongest feature: Sacks identifies the values he wants transcendence to preserve and explains why, after affirming science, he sees a moral function for a perspective beyond scientific description. Principal limitation: Difficulty finding scientific evidence for freedom, dignity, and hope does not establish that transcendence is necessary, and one behavioral psychologist cannot represent every secular account capable of grounding those values. Live burden: Sacks must compare his transcendent framework with nonreligious foundations, define what beyond us means, and connect that framework to preservation of the named values without treating science’s descriptive limits as theological evidence. Locked score: [withheld for blind rhetorical review].
